title: What time is it? — time and appointments
goal: Tell the time and make appointments — with সাড়ে for “half past”, special words for 1:30 and 2:30, and the part of the day placed before the hour.
bekal: ask কটা বাজে and answer it
use সাড়ে, সোয়া, and পৌনে for half and quarter hours
learn দেড়টা (1:30) and আড়াইটা (2:30), which have their own words
put সকাল, দুপুর, বিকেল, সন্ধ্যা, রাত before the hour
make an appointment with the -টায় ending

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — Making plans for tomorrow
dialogs.intro: Mitali invites Ani to the museum tomorrow. The conversation is full of clock times. Watch the word **সাড়ে**: it means “half past”, never “half to”.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Do you want to go to the museum tomorrow? In the morning?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: We'll leave at half past ten. OK?
lines.literal: half-past — ten-o'clock-at — out — will-become. fine — is?

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Half past ten — does that mean 9:30?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: No, no! Half past ten means 10:30. After ten.
lines.literal: no — no! half-past — ten-o'clock — meaning — ten-o'clock — thirty. ten-'s — after.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Oh! In Indonesia we say it the other way round.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Really? Then be careful! And we'll come back at 1:30.
lines.literal: so — is-it? if-so — careful! and — one-and-a-half-at — will-return.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: No, one and two have their own words: deṛ and aṛai.
lines.literal: no, one-o'clock — and — two-o'clock-'s — for — separate — word — is: one-and-a-half — and — two-and-a-half.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I'm writing that down. What time does the museum close?
lines.literal: writing — am-keeping. museum — when — closed — becomes?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: At five in the afternoon. We have three hours.
lines.literal: afternoon — five-o'clock-at. our — three — hour — time — is.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: That's plenty! I won't be late, I promise.
lines.literal: enough! I — delay — will-do — not, word — gave.

notes: **সাড়ে তিনটা is 3:30 — “half past three”, just as in English.** The rule: **সাড়ে + number = that hour plus thirty minutes.** সাড়ে ছটা = 6:30. সাড়ে নটা = 9:30. Ani stumbles because Indonesian (like German *halb vier*) names the **coming** hour; for English speakers, Bengali counts the familiar way.

⚠️ **1:30 and 2:30 have their own words, and সাড়ে can't be used for them.** 1:30 is **দেড়টা** *déRTa*, 2:30 is **আড়াইটা** *aRaiTa*. Saying *সাড়ে একটা* or *সাড়ে দুটো* sounds wrong at once. সাড়ে only kicks in from three: সাড়ে তিনটা, সাড়ে চারটা, and so on.

**Quarter hours have their own two words too: সোয়া and পৌনে.** **সোয়া** *soa* means “quarter past”: সোয়া তিনটা = 3:15. **পৌনে** *pouné* means “quarter to”: পৌনে চারটা = 3:45 — here the number named is the **coming** hour, the opposite of সাড়ে. If confused, just say the plain numbers: তিনটা পঁয়তাল্লিশ (3:45). Everyone understands.

**The part of the day comes first, then the hour.** সকাল আটটা (8 a.m., literally “morning eight”), দুপুর বারোটা (12 noon), বিকেল পাঁচটা (5 p.m.), রাত নটা (9 p.m.). ⚠️ This is the reverse of English “eight in the morning”. Bengali has no a.m./p.m.; the part-of-day word does that job.

**Bengal divides the day into more parts than English.** ভোর *bhor* (dawn, before sunrise), সকাল *sôkal* (morning), দুপুর *dupur* (midday), বিকেল *bikél* (afternoon), সন্ধ্যা *sôndha* (dusk), রাত *rat* (night). ⚠️ সন্ধ্যা has a special place in Bengali life: it's when lamps are lit, prayers are said, and guests start arriving.

**To say “at … o'clock”, add the place ending you already know: -য়.** তিনটা → **তিনটায়** (at three), সাড়ে দশটা → **সাড়ে দশটায়**, পাঁচটা → **পাঁচটায়**. It's the same ending as “at home” and “in Dhaka” — Bengali treats time as a place.

⚠️ **কটা বাজে? literally means “how many are striking?”** — from the bells once rung for each hour. The answer uses the same word: তিনটা বাজে (it's three o'clock). Don't be puzzled by বাজা (to strike, ring) in talk about time; it has nothing to do with music.

grammars.title: Telling the time
after: **When in doubt, say the plain numbers.** সাড়ে, সোয়া, and পৌনে are more natural, but **আটটা পনেরো** (8:15) and **নটা পঁয়তাল্লিশ** (9:45) are used every day — especially at stations, airports, and formal appointments. No one will find it odd.

grammars.title: Parts of the day and time words
after: ⚠️ **কাল means both yesterday AND tomorrow** — the verb decides which. কাল এসেছি (I came yesterday) versus কাল যাব (I'll go tomorrow). To be explicit, people add **গতকাল** (*gôtôkal* — yesterday) or **আগামীকাল** (*agamikal* — tomorrow). Unit 10 goes further.

blocks.title: ⚠️ About time and patience
items: **Appointment times in Bengal often come with a margin**, especially for informal plans. “সাড়ে পাঁচটায় আসছি” can mean anywhere between 5:30 and 6:00. It isn't rudeness but a shared, understood habit.
**For official matters, on the other hand, be on time.** Offices, interviews, and doctor's appointments run by the clock. A safe phrase: **আমি ঠিক সময়ে আসব** (*Thik sô-mô-yé* — I'll come on time).

**If you're running late, say so early; don't stay silent.** One short message, **একটু দেরি হচ্ছে, দুঃখিত** (running a bit late, sorry), is enough, and far more appreciated than a long explanation after you arrive.

blocks.text: One nice thing about the word **সময়** *sômôy*. It means “time”, but also “chance” and “era” — সময় নেই (there's no time), সময় হলে (if there's a chance), সেই সময় (in those days). And there's an expression you'll often hear from older people: **সময়মতো** *sômôy-môto*, “in due time” — the answer given when someone is too impatient for something.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

items: Come at five in the afternoon.

answers: সাড়ে চারটা — দেড়টা — আড়াইটা — সোয়া সাতটা — সকাল আটটা
কটা বাজে? — আমি সাড়ে দশটায় যাব। — জাদুঘর বিকেল পাঁচটায় বন্ধ হয়। — আমাদের তিন ঘণ্টা সময় আছে। — আমি দেরি করব না।
এখন কটা বাজে? — এখন সাড়ে তিনটা বাজে। — বিকেল পাঁচটায় আসুন। — আমি একটু দেরি করব। — কতক্ষণ লাগবে? — আগামীকাল সকালে আমরা বের হব।
